title: Trump FCC kills TV ownership cap, claiming authority over limit set by Congress
gist: The FCC voted 2-1 on August 6, 2026 to eliminate the National Television Ownership Rule that barred any single broadcast owner from reaching more than 39 percent of US TV households, replacing it with case-by-case merger review. The legal core of the story is whether the FCC can undo a cap Congress wrote into statute in 2004 — a question now decided without Chevron deference — and Free Press has said it will sue, making the deregulation contingent on courts rather than settled.

insights.claim: The FCC voted 2-1 on August 6, 2026 to eliminate the National Television Ownership Rule, which barred any single broadcast station owner from reaching more than 39 percent of US TV households.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Removes the hard statutory ceiling that has capped the maximum size of any US broadcast station group, opening the theoretical path to national-scale roll-ups.
insights.quote: The Federal Communications Commission voted 2–1 today to eliminate the National Television Ownership Rule, claiming authority to repeal a limit that was set by Congress over 20 years ago.
insights.locator: The Federal Communications Commission voted 2–1 today

insights.claim: Rather than raising the national TV household reach limit to a new number, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr is replacing the bright-line 39 percent rule with discretionary case-by-case review of each proposed broadcast merger.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Deal outcomes shift from a mechanical arithmetic test to regulator discretion, so political alignment of an acquirer becomes a material variable in broadcast M&A underwriting.
insights.quote: This will empower the FCC to approve deals that promote the public interest while allowing the agency to reject any deals that do not meet that standard,
insights.locator: Under Chairman Brendan Carr, the FCC is replacing

insights.claim: The FCC's stated justification for scrapping the national ownership cap is that broadcasters need scale to compete with streaming companies, which face no equivalent reach limits.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The regulatory rationale explicitly benchmarks legacy broadcast against streaming, signaling that further broadcast-favoring deregulation will be argued on the same asymmetry.
insights.locator: Without the 39 percent rule, broadcasters will be better able to compete

insights.claim: Carr frames consolidation as pro-local-news, arguing that local broadcast stations have degenerated into 'undifferentiated passthroughs of national programming produced in Hollywood and New York' and that larger scale would let them attract capital and ad revenue for community journalism.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Watch whether post-merger station groups actually increase local news spend — the public-interest justification is the record courts will scrutinize.
insights.quote: Increased scale will enable broadcasters to attract the capital and advertising revenue needed to sustain and produce trusted and community-focused news and programming.
insights.locator: Repealing the national cap will provide essential relief

insights.claim: Congress directed the FCC to set the national TV ownership cap at 39 percent in 2004, overriding a 2003 FCC decision that had raised the limit from 35 to 45 percent, and the same 2004 law barred the FCC from repealing or modifying the cap during its quadrennial media-rule reviews.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The explicit statutory anti-modification language is the central litigation risk that could unwind any merger consummated under the repeal.
insights.locator: For courts, the main question will be whether the FCC can change the cap at all

insights.claim: Carr's legal workaround is procedural rather than substantive: he is betting courts will hold that the FCC may eliminate the cap so long as it acts outside the quadrennial review process that the 2004 statute restricted.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The repeal's survival hinges on a narrow procedural reading, a thinner reed than a merits defense and a plausible point of judicial failure.
insights.locator: Carr is hoping courts will decide that the FCC can eliminate the cap

insights.claim: The DC Circuit precedent Carr cites — that Congress's chosen percentage set 'only the starting point from which the Commission was to assess the need for further change' — is a 2002 ruling about the earlier 35 percent cap, issued before Congress set 39 percent and restricted the FCC's ability to change it.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The author is flagging that the agency's headline precedent is materially weaker than presented — a direct signal that the repeal is more likely to be vacated than the FCC's confidence implies.

insights.claim: The 2024 Supreme Court decision overturning Chevron deference removes the interpretive cushion agencies previously relied on, so courts reviewing the FCC's cap repeal can decide for themselves what Congress meant without deferring to the agency.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Post-Chevron, aggressive agency reinterpretations of statutory numbers carry higher reversal risk — a generalizable handicap for any deal built on this kind of deregulation.
insights.locator: Another problem for Carr is the 2024 Supreme Court ruling

insights.claim: Prominent Republicans — former FCC Commissioner Mike O'Rielly, former House Majority Leader Tom DeLay who negotiated the 39 percent compromise, and Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz — have all said the FCC lacks authority to change the cap without Congress.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Opposition spanning both parties, including the Senate committee chair with jurisdiction, weakens the odds of a legislative rescue if courts strike the repeal down.
insights.quote: Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz has said he is ‘skeptical a change can be made absent an act of Congress.’
insights.locator: It’s worth noting that Republicans with deep firsthand knowledge

insights.claim: Free Press has said it will sue the FCC to block the repeal, meaning the elimination of the 39 percent cap is not operative-until-final but immediately contested in court.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Any broadcast deal signed against the new regime carries litigation-contingency risk and should be priced with a reversal scenario.
insights.quote: Changing this limit requires congressional action, but Carr doesn’t care,
insights.locator: Media advocacy group Free Press said it will sue

themes.theme: Consolidation and political leverage over broadcasters

insights.claim: Removing the 39 percent reach cap makes it easier for the FCC to approve broadcast mergers that produce news coverage more favorable to President Trump, in an agency where the chairman has repeatedly threatened to revoke licenses of broadcasters who drew Trump's ire.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: License risk and editorial alignment become priced variables for owners of national broadcast assets, not abstract political noise.
insights.quote: Carr has consistently threatened to revoke licenses from broadcasters who have drawn Trump’s ire, including by ordering an early license review of all ABC-owned stations.
insights.locator: The change, if not stopped by courts, will make it easier

insights.claim: Free Press predicts the repeal's endgame is one or two dominant broadcasters in every US market, accompanied by deep journalist job cuts and cheap national content repackaged as local news.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: If the repeal survives, expect station-group cost synergies to come disproportionately from newsroom headcount — a margin tailwind for acquirers and a structural decline in local news supply.
insights.quote: The result would be just one or two dominant broadcasters in every market, deep job cuts for journalists, and an influx of bargain-basement content disguised as local news.
insights.locator: He’ll do whatever it takes to clear the way

insights.claim: Carr already waived the TV ownership rule to approve Nexstar Media Group's purchase of Tegna, which pushed Nexstar's reach above half of US TV households, and that merger is now being challenged in court.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Nexstar-Tegna is the live test case: the cap repeal effectively retroactively legitimizes a deal already operating above the old limit and under legal attack.
insights.locator: Carr previously waived the TV ownership rule

insights.claim: A federal judge has ordered Nexstar and Tegna to stop integrating their assets and operations while an antitrust lawsuit filed by DirecTV proceeds.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Synergy realization at Nexstar-Tegna is judicially frozen, so modeled deal accretion should be pushed out or haircut pending the DirecTV antitrust case.
insights.locator: A federal judge ordered the companies to stop integrating

insights.claim: Nexstar backed Carr when he threatened ABC station licenses and urged stations to stop carrying Jimmy Kimmel's show, illustrating that station groups with pending regulatory approvals have incentives to align editorially with the FCC chairman.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Case-by-case merger review converts programming decisions into regulatory currency — a mechanism to watch as more deals queue up.
insights.locator: Nexstar sided with Carr last year

insights.claim: Both Democratic and Republican FCC leaderships have previously claimed authority to change the national ownership cap as long as they acted outside the quadrennial review, but Carr is the first chairman to test whether the FCC can eliminate the cap entirely.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Prior bipartisan practice supports modification, not abolition — the legal gap between those two acts is where this repeal is most exposed.
insights.quote: An unbroken line of FCC chairs going back more than a dozen years all agreed that the FCC has the authority to modify the cap
insights.locator: Both Democratic and Republican FCC leaders have claimed authority

insights.claim: The prior precedent cuts in both directions: Democratic Chairman Tom Wheeler used the same asserted authority to make the cap stricter by eliminating the UHF discount that counts only half the households reached by UHF stations, and Republican Chairman Ajit Pai reinstated the discount the following year.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The reach math itself is politically reversible chair-to-chair, so ownership-cap headroom is a policy variable with a roughly four-year half-life rather than a durable asset.
insights.locator: The Wheeler FCC tried to make the cap stricter

themes.theme: Dissent: who actually squeezes local stations

insights.claim: Democratic FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez voted against the repeal and argued Congress deliberately enshrined the 39 percent cap in statute and removed it from the Commission's review process, so only Congress can change it.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The dissent lays out the roadmap plaintiffs will use in court, which is the near-term binary for broadcast M&A.
insights.locator: Democratic FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez voted against

insights.claim: Gomez argues that eliminating the cap does not relieve local broadcasters from competitive strain — it only transfers the squeeze from digital giants to a handful of national station-group owners that increasingly dictate what airs on local stations without local input.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Undercuts the 'scale saves local news' thesis: the economic beneficiary is the station-group consolidator, not the local outlet, which is where the value accrual actually sits.
insights.quote: Trading a squeeze from Big Tech for a squeeze from Big Media does nothing to protect the communities this cap was designed to serve.
insights.locator: Digital giants compete for their most valuable programming
